title: Numeric Patterns: Rules, Tables and Flow Diagrams
seo_title: Grade 5 Numeric Patterns Worksheets with Answers (CAPS Maths)
standard_text: Investigate and extend numeric patterns looking for relationships or rules of patterns: sequences involving a constant difference or ratio, and of the learner's own creation; describe the general rules for the observed relationships; determine input values, output values and rules for the patterns and relationships using flow diagrams and tables.
meta_desc: Free CAPS Grade 5 numeric patterns worksheets: constant difference and ratio, pattern rules, input and output tables and flow diagrams. 100 questions with memos.
key_big: Find the rule and test it on every term.
key_sub: Constant difference: + or −. Constant ratio: × or ÷.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • A pattern can add or subtract the same number each time (constant difference): 7, 15, 23, 31 …
  • Or multiply by the same number each time (constant ratio): 3, 6, 12, 24 …
  • Check the rule with every pair of terms, not just the first two.
  • A flow diagram takes an input, does the operations in order, and gives the output.

Examples

Example

4, 12, 36, 108, …

each term × 3

Answer: 324

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Adding instead of multiplyingCheck the difference between more terms.
First two terms onlyTest the rule on all the terms.
Wrong orderFollow the arrows.

faq.q: What does CAPS Grade 5 say about numeric patterns?
faq.a: Investigate and extend numeric patterns with a constant difference or ratio, or of the learner's own creation, describe the rules, and use flow diagrams and tables.
Multiplying by the same number each time.
A diagram with arrows that shows the input, the operations and the output.

faq.q: How do I find a missing input?
faq.a: Work backwards with the inverse operations.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 3. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 6. What number goes in the ? box?
items.e: Pattern B adds 6 each time. The term before the ? is 6, so 6 + 6 = 12. (Adding 3 uses the rule of the other pattern.)

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 2. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 8. What number goes in the ? box?
items.e: Pattern B adds 8 each time. The term before the ? is 16, so 16 + 8 = 24. (Adding 2 uses the rule of the other pattern.)

items.e: Pattern A adds 4 each time. The term before the ? is 8, so 8 + 4 = 12. (Adding 12 uses the rule of the other pattern.)

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 4. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 8. Which list shows the first five terms of Pattern B?

items.q:
Which list follows the pattern rule?
Start at 6 and add 4 each time.
items.e: Start at 6, then add 4: 6, 10, 14, 18. (4, 10, 16, 22 swaps the numbers: it starts at 4 and adds 6.)

items.q:
Which list follows the pattern rule?
Start at 25 and add 5 each time.
items.e: Start at 25, then add 5: 25, 30, 35, 40. (5, 30, 55, 80 swaps the numbers: it starts at 5 and adds 25.)

items.q:
Which list follows the pattern rule?
Start at 90 and subtract 8 each time.
items.e: Start at 90, then subtract 8: 90, 82, 74, 66. The first term is the start number, 90. (90, 98, 106, 114 adds instead of subtracting.)

items.q:
Which pattern rule describes this pattern?
5, 10, 15, 20, …
c: Start at 5 and multiply by 2 each time.
Start at 5 and add 5 each time.
Start at 10 and add 5 each time.
Start at 5 and add 10 each time.
items.e: Each term is 5 more than the one before. “Multiply by 2” works for 5 → 10, but not for 10 → 15.

items.q:
Which pattern rule describes this pattern?
6, 18, 30, 42, …
c: Start at 12 and add 6 each time.
Start at 18 and add 12 each time.
Start at 6 and add 12 each time.
Start at 6 and multiply by 3 each time.
items.e: Each term is 12 more than the one before. “Multiply by 3” works for 6 → 18, but 18 × 3 is 54, not 30.

items.q:
Which pattern rule describes this pattern?
250, 235, 220, 205, …
c: Start at 250 and subtract 25 each time.
Start at 235 and subtract 15 each time.
Start at 250 and subtract 15 each time.
Start at 250 and add 15 each time.
items.e: The terms get smaller, so the rule subtracts. 250 − 15 = 235, 235 − 15 = 220. The start is the first term, 250.

items.q:
Which pattern rule describes this pattern?
3, 6, 12, 24, …
c: Start at 3 and add 3 each time.
Start at 3 and multiply by 2 each time.
Start at 3 and add 6 each time.
Start at 6 and multiply by 2 each time.
items.e: Each term is 2 times the one before: 3 × 2 = 6, 6 × 2 = 12, 12 × 2 = 24. “Add 3” works only for the first step.

items.q:
Which pattern rule describes this pattern?
400, 200, 100, 50, …
c: Start at 200 and divide by 2 each time.
Start at 400 and subtract 100 each time.
Start at 400 and divide by 2 each time.
Start at 400 and subtract 200 each time.
items.e: Each term is half of the one before: 400 ÷ 2 = 200, 200 ÷ 2 = 100, 100 ÷ 2 = 50. “Subtract 200” works only for the first step.

items.q:
What is the missing term?
500, 475, ?, 425, 400
items.e: The rule subtracts 25 each time. The missing term is 475 − 25 = 450. Check: 450 − 25 = 425. (The gap from 475 to 425 is 2 jumps, not 1.)

items.q:
What is the missing term?
15, ?, 29, 36, 43
items.e: The rule adds 7 each time. The missing term is 15 + 7 = 22. Check: 22 + 7 = 29. (The gap from 15 to 29 is 2 jumps, not 1.)

items.q:
Which pattern rule describes this pattern?
2, 4, 8, 16, …
c: Start at 2 and add 2 each time.
Start at 4 and multiply by 2 each time.
Start at 2 and multiply by 2 each time.
Start at 2 and add 4 each time.
items.e: Each term is 2 times the one before: 2 × 2 = 4, 4 × 2 = 8, 8 × 2 = 16. “Add 2” works only for the first step.

items.q:
Which pattern rule describes this pattern?
3, 9, 15, 21, …
c: Start at 9 and add 6 each time.
Start at 3 and multiply by 3 each time.
Start at 6 and add 3 each time.
Start at 3 and add 6 each time.
items.e: Each term is 6 more than the one before. “Multiply by 3” works for 3 → 9 but not for 9 → 15.

items.q:
Which pattern rule describes this pattern?
96, 48, 24, 12, …
c: Start at 48 and divide by 2 each time.
Start at 96 and subtract 48 each time.
Start at 96 and subtract 24 each time.
Start at 96 and divide by 2 each time.
items.e: Each term is half of the one before: 96 ÷ 2 = 48, 48 ÷ 2 = 24, 24 ÷ 2 = 12. “Subtract 48” works only for the first step.

items.q:
Which pattern rule describes this pattern?
100, 93, 86, 79, …
c: Start at 100 and subtract 7 each time.
Start at 93 and subtract 7 each time.
Start at 100 and add 7 each time.
Start at 79 and subtract 7 each time.
items.e: The first term is 100, and each term is 7 less than the one before: 100 − 7 = 93, 93 − 7 = 86.

items.q:
Which pattern rule describes this pattern?
4, 8, 12, 16, …
c: Start at 4 and add 4 each time.
Start at 4 and add 8 each time.
Start at 4 and multiply by 2 each time.
Start at 8 and add 4 each time.
items.e: Each term is 4 more than the one before. “Multiply by 2” works for 4 → 8 but not for 8 → 12.

items.q: Which rule gives the term value from the term number?
items.e: The term value goes up by 5, so multiply the term number by 5. Term 1: 1 × 5 = 5, and the value is 3, so subtract 2. Check term 4: 4 × 5 − 2 = 18. (A rule must work for every term, not only term 1.)

items.q: Which rule gives the term value from the term number?
items.e: The term value goes up by 4, so multiply the term number by 4. Term 1: 1 × 4 = 4, and the value is 7, so add 3. Check term 4: 4 × 4 + 3 = 19. (A rule must work for every term, not only term 1.)

items.q: Which rule gives the term value from the term number?
items.e: The term value goes up by 2, so multiply the term number by 2. Term 1: 1 × 2 = 2, and the value is 7, so add 5. Check term 4: 4 × 2 + 5 = 13. (A rule must work for every term, not only term 1.)

items.q: Which rule gives the term value from the term number?
items.e: The term value goes up by 3, so multiply the term number by 3. Term 1: 1 × 3 = 3, and the value is 4, so add 1. Check term 4: 4 × 3 + 1 = 13. (A rule must work for every term, not only term 1.)

items.q: Which rule gives the term value from the term number?
items.e: The term value goes up by 10, so multiply the term number by 10. Term 1: 1 × 10 = 10, and the value is 15, so add 5. Check term 4: 4 × 10 + 5 = 45. (A rule must work for every term, not only term 1.)

items.q: Lerato builds a row of triangles with toothpicks. 1 triangle uses 3, 2 triangles use 5 and 3 triangles use 7. How many toothpicks does she need for 20 triangles?
items.e: Each new triangle adds 2 toothpicks (it shares a side). From 1 to 20 triangles there are 19 jumps: 3 + 19 × 2 = 41. (20 × 3 = 60 counts the shared sides twice.)

items.q: A SkyTrain arrives at a station every 4 minutes. The first train arrives at 7:02 a.m. When does the 6th train arrive?
items.e: From the 1st train to the 6th train there are 5 jumps of 4 minutes: 5 × 4 = 20 minutes. 7:02 + 20 minutes = 7:22 a.m. (7:26 a.m. uses 6 jumps.)

items.q: A rain barrel holds 180 ℓ of water. Thabo uses 15 ℓ each day to water his garden. The rule is 180 − 15 × □, where □ is the number of days. After how many days will 45 ℓ be left?
items.e: He uses 180 − 45 = 135 ℓ. 135 ÷ 15 = 9 days. Check: 180 − 15 × 9 = 45. (45 ÷ 15 = 3 uses the water left, not the water used.)

items.q: In a school gym, chairs are set up for a concert. Row 1 has 18 chairs, and each row has 2 more chairs than the row before. How many chairs are in row 12?
items.e: From row 1 to row 12 there are 11 jumps: 18 + 11 × 2 = 40 chairs. (42 uses 12 jumps.)

items.q: Each point is (day, height). Which point will come next on the graph?
items.e: The next day is day 5. The height goes up 3 cm: 13 + 3 = 16. The point is (5, 16). (In (16, 5) the numbers are swapped: the day comes first.)

items.q: Thabo makes a row of squares with craft sticks: 4 sticks, 7 sticks, 10 sticks, … The rule is 3n + 1. Which figure uses 46 sticks?
items.e: 46 − 1 = 45, and 45 ÷ 3 = 15. So n = 15. Check: 3 × 15 + 1 = 46. (46 is the number of sticks, not the figure number.)

items.q: Square tables are pushed together in a row for a class party. 1 table seats 4 learners, 2 tables seat 6, and 3 tables seat 8. How many learners can sit at 12 tables?
items.e: Each new table adds 2 seats. From 1 table to 12 tables there are 11 jumps: 4 + 11 × 2 = 26. (12 × 4 = 48 counts seats that are lost where the tables touch.)

items.q: Palesa’s bean plant grows the same amount each day. How tall will it be on day 9?
items.e: It grows 3 cm a day. From day 1 to day 9 there are 8 jumps: 4 + 8 × 3 = 28 cm. (31 cm uses 9 jumps; 16 cm is day 5.)

items.q: Dumisani plants cedar seedlings in rows. Row 1 has 5 seedlings, row 2 has 9 and row 3 has 13. Which row has 61 seedlings?
items.e: The rows go up by 4. 61 − 5 = 56, and 56 ÷ 4 = 14 jumps after row 1, so it is row 15. (14 is the number of jumps, not the row number.)

items.q: Ethan has 150 pages left in his book. He reads 12 pages each day. How many pages are left after 9 days?
items.e: He reads 9 × 12 = 108 pages. 150 − 108 = 42 pages left. (108 is the pages he read, not the pages left.)

items.q: A lemonade recipe uses 1 cup of lemon juice for every 4 cups of water. Lemon juice: 1, 2, 3, … cups. Water: 4, 8, 12, … cups. How many cups of water go with 5 cups of lemon juice?
items.e: The water pattern adds 4 and the juice pattern adds 1, so the water is always 4 times the juice: 5 × 4 = 20 cups. (5 + 4 = 9 adds instead of multiplying.)

items.q: A lemonade recipe uses 1 cup of lemon juice for every 4 cups of water. The ordered pairs are (cups of lemon juice, cups of water). Which ordered pair fits the recipe?
items.e: 3 cups of juice need 3 × 4 = 12 cups of water. Juice comes first: (3, 12). (3, 7) adds 4 instead.

items.q: Two empty tanks are filled with water. Tank A gets 25 litres each minute and tank B gets 100 litres each minute. When tank A has 500 litres, how much does tank B have?
items.e: 100 = 4 × 25, and both start empty, so tank B always has 4 times as much: 500 × 4 = 2 000 litres.

items.q: Sarah is 8 years old and her brother is 5. Each year, both get 1 year older. How old will Sarah be when her brother is 12?
items.e: Sarah is 3 years older (8 − 5 = 3), and both add 1 each year, so she stays 3 years older: 12 + 3 = 15. (12 × 3 = 36 treats it as times.)

items.q: Sarah is 8 years old and her brother is 5. Why will Sarah always be 3 years older than her brother?
c: Sarah's age is 3 times his age
Sarah gets 3 years older each year
Both get 1 year older each year
items.e: The difference starts at 8 − 5 = 3. Each year both ages add the same number, 1, so the difference stays 3: 8 and 5, 9 and 6, 10 and 7.

items.q: Amahle swims 2 laps each day and Kabelo swims 6 laps each day. They start on the same day. When Kabelo has swum 42 laps in all, how many laps has Amahle swum?
items.e: 6 = 3 × 2, so Kabelo's total is always 3 times Amahle's. Work backward: 42 ÷ 3 = 14 laps. (Both have swum for 7 days: 7 × 2 = 14.)

items.q: A motorcycle has 2 wheels and a car has 4 wheels. The ordered pairs are (wheels on the motorcycles, wheels on the cars) for the same number of each. Which ordered pair is for 7 motorcycles and 7 cars?
items.e: 7 motorcycles have 7 × 2 = 14 wheels and 7 cars have 7 × 4 = 28 wheels: (14, 28). (7, 28) uses the number of motorcycles, not their wheels, and (2, 4) is for only 1 of each.

items.q: Lerato's pattern starts at 0 and adds 4. Sibusiso wants each term of his pattern to be 3 times the matching term of Lerato's. His pattern also starts at 0. Which rule should he use?
items.e: Each step Sibusiso must add 3 times as much as Lerato: 3 × 4 = 12. Check: 4 and 12, 8 and 24, 12 and 36. (Add 7 is 4 + 3.)

items.q: Precious's Pattern A starts at 2 and adds 6. She wants each term of Pattern B to be 5 more than the matching A term. Which start and rule should Pattern B have?
items.e: To stay 5 more, B must start 5 higher (2 + 5 = 7) and grow by the same amount, 6. Adding 11 each time would make the difference grow: 7 and 2, 18 and 8.

items.q: Printer A prints 120 pages each minute and printer B prints 480 pages each minute. They start at the same time. When printer A has printed 1 080 pages, how many has printer B printed?
items.e: 480 = 4 × 120, so printer B always prints 4 times as many pages: 1 080 × 4 = 4 320 pages.
